Using $K$-fold cross-fitting, CF-NPE fits $K$ posterior-mean regressors and then fits a conditional density estimator to the resulting out-of-fold residuals. In experiments with synthetic data and in a cosmological application, CF-NPE achieves higher held-out log-likelihood than standard NPE and typically improves calibration. CF-NPE is most useful in high-dimensional, simulation-limited settings.
item.dc:creator: Jeffrey Regier

item.title: High-dimensional covariate-assisted ranking
item.description: arXiv:2610.26796v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Ranking data in modern applications often involves covariate vectors whose dimension grows with the number of objects. Identifying relevant covariates and integrating them with item-specific utilities can yield better predictive performance. In this work, we study a Plackett--Luce model that incorporates both item-specific utilities and high-dimensional covariate effects. Under a sparsity assumption on the covariate coefficients, we establish a necessary and sufficient condition for identifiability in terms of the Kruskal rank of the restricted covariate design. We then propose an $\ell_1$-regularized maximum likelihood estimator for the covariate coefficients. Under suitable design and connectivity conditions, we establish the existence and uniqueness of the estimator with probability tending to one, as well as its uniform consistency. With an additional minimum-signal condition, we further establish exact support recovery. Our analysis combines a hypergraph-based chaining technique with a profile-likelihood perturbation analysis, yielding estimation rates that explicitly capture the effects of the comparison hypergraph's connectivity and the underlying sparsity level. Numerical experiments using synthetic data and a horse racing dataset corroborate our theoretical findings.
item.dc:creator: Yujia Liu, Yuanyuan Lin, Ruijian Han, Yiming Xu

item.title: Learning to Refer: Inference-Time Collaboration in Decentralized Federated Learning
item.description: arXiv:2610.26800v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: In decentralized federated learning, heterogeneous clients may develop complementary expertise, yet each query is typically evaluated only by the client where it arrives. To exploit this distributed expertise without global coordination, we formulate inference-time collaboration as budgeted local expert referral, a graph-constrained routing process in which a query can move only between neighboring clients and only visited clients contribute to its final prediction. EdgeDRM implements this framework by learning a density-based routing potential for each client: differences between neighboring potentials provide the comparisons used to select successive referrals, while local task models generate predictions that are aggregated along the resulting route. Both training and inference are decentralized, using only neighbor-local information without a central router or graph-wide client scoring. We establish estimation guarantees for the learned comparisons and characterize how local improvement and graph structure govern prior-weighted density gains from referral. Experiments on benchmark and real-world medical data show that EdgeDRM outperforms graph-matched decentralized baselines in most settings, with the clearest benefits under sparse connectivity.
item.dc:creator: Yuheng Ma, Chendi Wang, Qiong Zhang

item.title: Reinforcement Learning for Individual Optimal Policy from Heterogeneous Data
item.description: arXiv:2505.09496v4 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Offline reinforcement learning (RL) aims to find optimal policies in dynamic environments in order to maximize the expected total rewards by leveraging pre-collected data. Learning from heterogeneous data is one of the fundamental challenges in offline RL. Traditional methods focus on learning an optimal policy for all individuals with pre-collected data from a single episode or homogeneous batch episodes, and thus, may result in a suboptimal policy for a heterogeneous population. In this paper, we propose an individualized offline policy optimization framework for heterogeneous time-stationary Markov decision processes (MDPs). The proposed heterogeneous model with individual latent variables enables us to efficiently estimate the individual Q-functions, and our Penalized Pessimistic Personalized Policy Learning (P4L) algorithm guarantees a fast rate on the average regret under a weak partial coverage assumption on behavior policies. In addition, our simulation studies and a real data application demonstrate the superior numerical performance of the proposed method compared with existing methods.
item.dc:creator: Rui Miao, Babak Shahbaba, Annie Qu

item.title: Generative Flows for Potential Outcomes and Counterfactuals
item.description: arXiv:2505.16051v5 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Average treatment effects summarize how interventions change outcomes, but individualized decisions require predictions and outcome distributions of what would have happened to the same individual under an alternative treatment. We develop PO-Flow, a continuous normalizing flow framework that represents treatment-specific outcome distributions through invertible transport maps. It supports potential-outcome generation, conditional average treatment-effect estimation, factual-conditioned counterfactual prediction, and density evaluation. To address treatment imbalance in observational data, we incorporate cross-fitted inverse-probability weighting into the flow-matching loss. We establish sufficient conditions under which encoding a factual outcome and decoding under an alternative treatment recovers the individual counterfactual. Under shared exogenous noise and a common encoded reference distribution, scalar recovery follows from increasing noise-to-latent maps. For multivariate outcomes, we assume triangularity or a convex-gradient structure. These conditions distinguish fitting outcome distributions from recovering their causal correspondence. Experiments on four scalar benchmarks and seven multivariate or image settings, with dimensions up to 784, compare against ten scalar and five multivariate baselines. Controlled ablations show IPW improves all reported scalar counterfactual RMSE, PEHE, and potential-outcome RMSE. PO-Flow achieves the lowest PEHE and potential-outcome RMSE on all four scalar benchmarks and attains or ties the lowest mean in 26 of 35 multivariate dataset--metric comparisons.
item.dc:creator: Dongze Wu, David I. Inouye, Yao Xie

item.title: Smooth Flow Matching for Synthesizing Functional Data
item.description: arXiv:2508.13831v5 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Functional data, i.e., random functions observed over a continuous domain, are increasingly available in areas such as biomedical research, health informatics, and epidemiology. However, effective statistical analysis for functional data is often hindered by challenges such as privacy constraints, sparse and irregular sampling, infinite-dimensionality, and non-Gaussian structures. To address these challenges, we introduce a novel framework named Smooth Flow Matching (SFM), tailored for generative modeling of functional data that enables statistical analysis without exposing sensitive real data. Under a copula framework, SFM constructs a semiparametric smooth flow to generate infinite-dimensional functional data, free of Gaussianity and low-rank assumptions. It is computationally efficient, handles irregular observations, and guarantees the smoothness of the generated functions, offering a practical and flexible solution in scenarios where existing deep generative methods are not applicable. Through extensive simulation studies, we demonstrate the advantages of SFM in terms of both synthetic data quality and computational efficiency. We then apply SFM to generate clinical trajectory data from the MIMIC-IV patient electronic health records (EHR) longitudinal database. Our analysis showcases the ability of SFM to produce high-quality surrogate data for downstream tasks, highlighting its potential to boost the utility of EHR data for clinical applications.
item.dc:creator: Jianbin Tan, Anru R. Zhang

item.title: Hybrid Topic-Semantic Labeling and Graph Embeddings for Unsupervised Legal Document Clustering
item.description: arXiv:2509.00990v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Legal documents pose substantial challenges for unsupervised knowledge discovery due to specialized domain terminology, multi-scale document lengths, and scarce expert annotations. This paper introduces Topic-Graph Spherical Fusion (TGSF), a dual-manifold representation learning framework for unsupervised legal document clustering that unifies dense topic-semantic discovery and relational graph embeddings on a joint unit hypersphere. Instantiating dense topic discovery via Top2Vec and biased second-order random walks via Node2Vec, TGSF constructs a connected multi-relational document-topic graph combining multi-topic centroid bridges with temperature-sharpened semantic k-Nearest Neighbor (k-NN) document edges, guaranteeing a single connected component. The resulting L2-normalized semantic and graph representations are fused via modality-weighted concatenation onto a joint unit hypersphere prior to KMeans partitioning, decomposing squared chordal distance into a convex combination of semantic and structural cosine similarities. Evaluations across three legal benchmarks (ACORD, CUAD, and LEDGAR) show that TGSF outperforms semantic-only, structural-only, Latent Dirichlet Allocation (LDA), Non-Negative Matrix Factorization (NMF), and TF-IDF baselines. Across 216 factorial grid configurations and 240 Bayesian TPE and Multi-Objective NSGA-II Pareto optimization trials per dataset (720 trials total), TGSF improves Normalized Mutual Information (NMI) from 0.606 to 0.653 on LEDGAR (ARI = 0.425), 0.228 to 0.284 on ACORD (ARI = 0.260), and 0.535 to 0.570 on CUAD (ARI = 0.282). Functional ANOVA and Pareto frontier diagnostics further characterize hyperparameter sensitivity for reproducible legal text mining.
item.dc:creator: Deepak Bastola, Woohyeok Choi

item.title: Control Variate Design for Score-Function Gradient Estimators in Importance-Weighted Variational Inference
item.description: arXiv:2602.01412v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Importance-weighted variational inference approximates intractable densities by optimizing multi-sample Monte Carlo objectives whose tightness increases with the number of importance samples $N$. When reparameterization is unavailable, optimization relies on score-function (REINFORCE) gradient estimators. In this paper, we provide a comprehensive analysis of score-function gradient estimators for importance-weighted objectives by characterizing their asymptotic expectation and variance. We establish that standard variational inference for Monte Carlo objectives (VIMCO) gradient estimators suffer from a vanishing signal-to-noise ratio (SNR) as $N$ increases, which arises from a suboptimal control variate choice and can impair optimization. To address this issue, we derive a general mechanism for constructing VIMCO gradient estimators that avoid SNR collapse. We identify the High-Effective Sample Size optimal variance importance sampling estimator as belonging to this category of estimators and establish its $\sqrt{N}$ SNR scaling. This estimator does not, however, have zero variance at optimality and achieving its $\sqrt{N}$ SNR rate may require prohibitively large $N$ when the importance weights are degenerate. We overcome these limitations by introducing VIMCO gradient estimators that attain zero variance at optimality and support importance weight tempering. Experiments with discrete latent-variable and state-space models validate the theoretical predictions and illustrate the benefits of our estimators.
item.dc:creator: Kam\'elia Daudel, Minh-Ngoc Tran, Cheng Zhang

item.title: Statistical Inference and Learning for Shapley Additive Explanations (SHAP)
item.description: arXiv:2602.10532v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: The SHAP (short for Shapley additive explanation) framework has become an essential tool for attributing importance to variables in predictive tasks. In model-agnostic settings, SHAP uses the concept of Shapley values from cooperative game theory to fairly allocate credit to the features in a vector $X$ based on their contribution to an outcome $Y$. While the explanations offered by SHAP are local by nature, learners often need global measures of feature importance in order to improve model explainability and perform feature selection. The most common approach for converting these local explanations into global ones is to compute either the mean absolute SHAP or mean squared SHAP. However, despite their ubiquity, there do not exist approaches for performing statistical inference on these quantities. In this paper, we take a semi-parametric approach for calibrating confidence in estimates of the $p$th powers of Shapley additive explanations. We show that, by treating the SHAP curve as a nuisance function that must be estimated from data, one can reliably construct asymptotically normal estimates of the $p$th powers of SHAP. When $p \geq 2$, we show a de-biased estimator that combines U-statistics with Neyman orthogonal scores for functionals of nested regressions is asymptotically normal. When $1 \leq p < 2$ (and the hence target parameter is not twice differentiable), we construct de-biased U-statistics for a smoothed alternative. In particular, we show how to carefully tune the temperature parameter of the smoothing function in order to obtain inference for the true, unsmoothed $p$th power. We complement these results by presenting a Neyman orthogonal loss that can be used to learn the SHAP curve via empirical risk minimization and discussing excess risk guarantees for commonly used function classes.
item.dc:creator: Justin Whitehouse, Ayush Sawarni, Vasilis Syrgkanis

item.title: Post-Selection Distributional Model Evaluation
item.description: arXiv:2603.23055v4 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Formal model evaluation methods typically certify that a model satisfies a prescribed target key performance indicator (KPI) level. However, in many applications, the relevant target KPI level may not be known a priori, and the user may instead wish to compare candidate models by analyzing the full trade-offs between performance and reliability achievable at test time by the models. This task, requiring the reliable estimate of the test-time KPI distributions, is made more complicated by the fact that the same data must often be used both to pre-select a subset of candidate models and to estimate their KPI distributions, causing a potential post-selection bias. In this work, we introduce post-selection distributional model evaluation (PS-DME), a general framework for statistically valid distributional model assessment after arbitrary data-dependent model pre-selection. Building on e-values, PS-DME controls post-selection false coverage rate (FCR) for the distributional KPI estimates and we establish explicit conditions under which it is provably more sample efficient than a baseline method based on sample splitting. Experiments on synthetic data, text-to-SQL decoding with large language models, and telecom network performance evaluation demonstrate that PS-DME enables reliable comparison of candidate configurations across a range of reliability levels, supporting the statistically reliable exploration of performance--reliability trade-offs.
item.dc:creator: Amirmohammad Farzaneh, Osvaldo Simeone

item.title: A Transport Geometry of Benign Overfitting
item.description: arXiv:2604.08625v4 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Benign overfitting, the phenomenon that interpolating noisy data can be statistically harmless, is usually characterized through effective-rank conditions on the covariance spectrum. These conditions are fragile: a perturbation of vanishing relative operator and Frobenius norm can turn a benign covariance into one whose minimum-norm interpolator has non-vanishing excess risk. We argue that the natural geometry of benign overfitting is optimal transport of the log-eigenvalues, measured in units of the sample size $n$. In log-spectral coordinates, the deterministic equivalent of the risk becomes a functional of two measures smoothed by a logistic kernel centred at the interpolation threshold $\log\kappa$. We compute its exact first variation: the threshold moves by a sensitivity-weighted average of the log-eigenvalue displacements, and the influence of each eigenvalue decays exponentially with its log-distance to the threshold. We then derive global, dimension-free stability bounds. The variance functional is $8/(27n)$-Lipschitz in the 1-Wasserstein distance between log-spectra, with a sharp constant, and is controlled more generally by a threshold-localized transport discrepancy; an analogous bound controls the bias. Consequently, any rank-$k$ update of the covariance, of arbitrary norm, changes the variance functional by at most $3k/n$, and benign overfitting survives every perturbation whose localized transport cost is $o(n)$. The results extend to ridge regression and to infinite-dimensional trace-class covariances. Matching lower bounds show that the $n$-scaling is necessary and cannot be replaced by operator norms, Frobenius norms, or dimension-normalized spectral distances. Simulations, one-step feature learning in two-layer networks, and random features of real images support the theory and delineate its limits.
item.dc:creator: Olaf Yunus Laitinen Imanov, Rana Irem Turhan, Isgandar Jafarli

item.title: Best of both worlds: Stochastic & adversarial best-arm identification
item.description: arXiv:2604.14860v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: We study bandit best-arm identification with arbitrary and potentially adversarial rewards. A simple random uniform learner obtains the optimal rate of error in the adversarial scenario. However, this type of strategy is suboptimal when the rewards are sampled stochastically. Therefore, we ask: Can we design a learner that performs optimally in both the stochastic and adversarial problems while not being aware of the nature of the rewards? First, we show that designing such a learner is impossible in general. In particular, to be robust to adversarial rewards, we can only guarantee optimal rates of error on a subset of the stochastic problems. We give a lower bound that characterizes the optimal rate in stochastic problems if the strategy is constrained to be robust to adversarial rewards. Finally, we design a simple parameter-free algorithm and show that its probability of error matches (up to log factors) the lower bound in stochastic problems, and it is also robust to adversarial ones.
item.dc:creator: Yasin Abbasi-Yadkori, Peter L. Bartlett, Victor Gabillon, Alan Malek, Michal Valko

item.title: The Causal Description Gap: Information-Theoretic Separations Across Pearl's Hierarchy
item.description: arXiv:2605.02177v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Pearl's causal hierarchy shows that observational, interventional, and counterfactual queries are qualitatively distinct. We ask a quantitative version of this question: how many additional bits are needed to specify higher-rung causal answers once lower-rung answers are known? We formalize this via query-class description length, the Kolmogorov complexity of the answers a structural causal model (SCM) gives to a class of queries, with system size given. Our main construction gives acyclic SCMs on $n$ binary variables whose common observational distribution has constant description length, while single-variable intervention answers can require $\Theta(n^2)$ additional bits. For SCMs with independent noises, fixed finite gate-schema and noise libraries, and at most $d$ parents per variable, a degree-sensitive upper bound gives an observational-interventional gap of at most $O(nd\log(en/d)+n\log n)$. This makes the quadratic construction order-optimal in the dense regime and a rooted-tree construction order-optimal for bounded indegree. The quadratic separation persists under $\varepsilon$-accurate total-variation descriptions for every fixed $\varepsilon<1/4$. At the next rung, even knowing every hard-intervention distribution can leave a $\Theta(n)$ counterfactual description gap; a masked-parity construction extends this to $\Theta(n^2)$. These separation rates hold in the worst case and with high probability under uniform hidden parameters. A general ambiguity-to-bits theorem and Shannon analogue, together with explicit encodings, show that the gaps in our constructions equal the logarithm of residual higher-rung ambiguity up to lower-order terms.
item.dc:creator: Seyed Morteza Emadi

item.title: Regional summaries of Bayesian model uncertainty
item.description: arXiv:2606.21080v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Bayesian posterior uncertainty can be spread across many models that share the same substantive pattern. Lists of individual models can obscure this structure, while marginal summaries do not describe which configurations are jointly supported. We study how to represent joint model uncertainty through a compact collection of interpretable regions, each grouping models that share a specified pattern. We formulate this task as minimizing representation complexity subject to retaining a prescribed posterior mass within an analyst-supplied family. To address unknown regional probabilities, we develop Adaptive Regional Selection (ARS), which combines adaptive exploration and regional weight estimation with conservative and optimistic selection. These complementary problems identify a summary meeting the mass target and bound how much further its complexity could improve. Under valid regional bounds, we establish guarantees for retained mass, total-variation error, and suboptimality, together with conditions for certifying optimality. We also show that, under bounded within-region weight variation, sufficient sample counts for regional estimation need not grow with the number of represented models, and construct bounds that remain valid under adaptive sampling and stopping. Empirical studies illustrate regional summaries in Bayesian model averaging and Bayesian networks, examining retained mass, representation complexity, and certification.
item.dc:creator: Hanqing Li, Robert Nguyen, Xuewen Lu

item.title: FairBED: Incorporating Fairness into Bayesian Experimental Design
item.description: arXiv:2606.23515v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Bayesian experimental design (BED) has traditionally focused exclusively on collecting data that is maximally informative, with little consideration of other desirable dataset characteristics, such as fairness. We therefore extend BED to target data that is both informative and fair. To this end, we introduce FairBED, which provides a formalism for the fairness of datasets themselves by measuring how compatible they are with a fair world, in which the target quantity we wish to learn about is unrelated to the sensitive attributes we want to be fair to. We then use this to construct practical fairness-aware BED objectives that maximise expected information gain about the target variables, while penalising information about sensitive attributes and/or their coupling with the target. We further extend FairBED to active learning, and show empirically that models trained on data gathered using FairBED provide improved fairness-accuracy trade-offs compared to randomly acquired data and conventional BED.
item.dc:creator: Marcel Hedman, Emily Alger, Brieuc Lehmann, Chris Holmes, Tom Rainforth

item.title: A Splitting Method for SDE Terminal-Law Estimation
item.description: arXiv:2609.12513v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: In many settings involving stochastic differential equations (SDEs), including diffusion based generative AI, our aim is to accurately generate samples from a distribution. Typically, this is done by generating i.i.d. samples of the SDE. Given a fixed simulation budget, a reasonable way to gain efficiency may be to instead generate a tree of paths through appropriately split partial paths. This suggests improved performance, but one worries about the injected dependence. In this paper, we study this issue comprehensively. We develop a general method to construct the splitting design and analyze its performance for a broad class of error measures, giving insight into the elegant underlying structure in the problem. For the Kolmogorov-Smirnov (KS) distance and maximum mean discrepancy (MMD), we identify the limiting errors of the associated empirical distributions as the simulation budget increases to infinity. We characterize a splitting strategy motivated by a corresponding asymptotic optimization problem. Overall, we observe a 12-26% improvement in mean KS over i.i.d. samples in many settings. On CIFAR-10 and FFHQ, splitting lowers the MMD by 17-26% relative to i.i.d. samples.
item.dc:creator: Rushil Gupta, Sandeep Juneja

item.title: SNACK: A Sequential Notation Framework for Probabilistic Graph Generation
item.description: arXiv:2610.19781v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: We introduce SNACK, a string representation for probabilistic graph generation that enables sequence models to generate and model graphs with discrete node and edge features. SNACK linearizes graphs by encoding the nonzero entries of the lower-triangular adjacency matrix, establishing a bijective correspondence between valid sequences and ordered adjacency matrices. This design enables invalid logit masking to enforce structural constraints--such as chemical valence and ordering rules--guaranteeing 100% valid generated sequences. SNACK also enables principled string-based GFlowNet training by explicitly accounting for node-ordering symmetries. Across standard graph-generation tasks and molecular distribution-learning benchmarks, SNACK achieves competitive sample quality, while substantially improving the throughput of GFlowNet training relative to graph-based generation. Probing analyses further show that models trained on SNACK encode meaningful local and global graph structure despite receiving only sequential supervision. These results position SNACK as a practical framework for probabilistic graph generation with deep sequence models.
item.dc:creator: Hohyun Kim, Hyesung Kim, Min-hwan Oh, Seunggeun Lee

item.title: Task-aware Kernel Stein certificates for R\'{e}nyi differential privacy
item.description: arXiv:2610.23798v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: R\`enyi differential privacy, based on R\`enyi divergence, has become a notion of choice for privacy guarantees. However, outside the Gaussian setting, R\`enyi divergence can be difficult to compute. In particular, R\`enyi differential privacy guarantees that exploit task-specific information, as in R\`enyi Pufferfish privacy, can be challenging. Here we use kernel Stein discrepancies based on escort distributions to provide certificates for R\`enyi differential privacy. By designing the kernel to focus on the relevant privacy directions, we also derive task-aware privacy certificates. We provide exact identities for Gaussian and Laplace mechanisms and bounds for exponential mechanisms, with separate task-aware guarantees. A real data set example illustrates how the protected comparison set and the released subspace jointly determine the resulting certificates.
item.dc:creator: Leoni Carla Wirth, Tara Trauthwein, Gesine Reinert

item.title: A probability calibrator for machine-learning classifiers
item.description: arXiv:2302.10578v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: In fields such as medicine and drug discovery, the ultimate goal of a classification is not to guess a class, but to choose the optimal course of action among a set of possible ones, usually not in one-one correspondence with the set of classes. This decision-theoretic problem requires proper probabilities for the classes. Proper probabilities conditional on the features are computationally almost impossible to find in many important cases. The main idea of the present work is to calculate probabilities conditional not on the features, but on the trained classifier's output. This calculation is cheap, needs to be made only once, and provides an output-to-probability "calibrator" or "transducer" that can be applied to all future outputs of the classifier. In conjunction with problem-dependent utilities, the probabilities of the transducer allow us to find the optimal choice among the classes or among a set of more general decisions, by means of expected-utility maximization. This idea is demonstrated in a simplified drug-discovery problem with a highly imbalanced dataset. The transducer and utility maximization together always lead to improved results, sometimes close to theoretical maximum, for all sets of problem-dependent utilities. The one-time-only calculation of the transducer also provides, automatically: (i) a quantification of the uncertainty about the transducer itself; (ii) the expected utility of the augmented algorithm (including its uncertainty), which can be used for algorithm selection; (iii) the possibility of using the algorithm in a "generative mode", useful if the training dataset is biased.
item.dc:creator: K. Dyrland, A. S. Lundervold, P. G. L. Porta Mana

item.title: Interacting Annealed Importance Sampling via Population-Based MCMC Kernels
item.description: arXiv:2401.15645v3 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Sampling from a multimodal distribution is a fundamental and challenging problem in computational science and statistics. Among various approaches proposed for this task, one popular method is Annealed Importance Sampling (AIS). In this paper, we propose an interaction-based version of AIS by combining it with population-based Monte Carlo methods to improve its efficiency. By keeping track of an ensemble instead of a single sampler along some continuation path between the starting distribution and the target distribution, we take advantage of the interaction within the ensemble to encourage the exploration of undiscovered modes. Specifically, our main idea is to utilize either the snooker algorithm or the genetic algorithm used in Evolutionary Monte Carlo. We discuss how the proposed algorithm can be implemented and derive a partial differential equation governing the evolution of the ensemble under the continuous time and mean-field limit. We also test the efficiency of the proposed algorithm on various continuous and discrete distributions.
item.dc:creator: Haoxuan Chen, Lexing Ying

item.title: Mitigating Data Reconstruction Attacks in Federated Learning: Conditions, Bounds, and Theoretical Guarantees
item.description: arXiv:2407.16735v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Privacy attacks, particularly data reconstruction attacks, pose significant challenges to federated learning despite its promise in privacy-preserving collaborative training. This paper presents a comprehensive theoretical analysis of privacy leakage in federated learning through dual perspectives: linear algebra and optimization theory. By analyzing the client-update Jacobian, we identify conditions under which distinct data batches produce the same model update and derive a sufficient batch-size criterion for non-unique reconstruction. Through optimization theory, we establish a novel upper bound for privacy leakage that incorporates batch size, distortion extent, and other critical parameters. These theoretical insights elucidate the fundamental relationships between system parameters and privacy vulnerability, laying the groundwork for developing more robust privacy-preserving federated learning frameworks.
item.dc:creator: Xiaojin Zhang, Mingcong Xu, Wei Chen, Qiang Yang

item.title: Identifying Elasticities in Autocorrelated Time Series Using Causal Mechanism Graphs
item.description: arXiv:2409.15530v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Instrumental variable (IV) methods are widely used to estimate the price elasticity of demand from observational data. However, naive IV estimators may be inconsistent in settings with autocorrelated time series. We argue that causal graphs taking into account time structure can simplify IV identification and help select consistent estimators. More precisely, we propose to model equilibrium conditions using causal mechanism time graphs. These (acyclic) graphs allow us to maintain the assumption of a simultaneous determination of prices and quantities and come with an interpretable notion of intervention. They further allow us to exploit recent advances in graphical inference to derive valid IV estimators that are consistent under weak assumptions. Finally, we argue that observing significant differences between the estimates of presumably valid estimators can help to reject false model assumptions, thereby improving our understanding of underlying economic dynamics. We apply our approach to the German electricity market, estimating the price elasticity of demand from simulated and real-world data. The findings underscore the importance of accounting for structural autocorrelation in IV-based analysis.
item.dc:creator: Lion Hirth (Centre for Sustainability, Hertie School), Jonas Peters (Department of Mathematics, ETH Zurich), Oliver Ruhnau (Faculty of Management, Economics and Social Sciences, Institute of Energy Economics, University of Cologne), Jorge S\'anchez Canales (Centre for Sustainability, Hertie School), Felix Schur (Department of Mathematics, ETH Zurich), Raffaele Sgarlato (Centre for Sustainability, Hertie School), Silvana Tiedemann (Centre for Sustainability, Hertie School)

item.title: Enhancing Offline Model-Based RL via Active Model Selection: A Bayesian Optimization Perspective
item.description: arXiv:2502.11480v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Offline model-based reinforcement learning (MBRL) serves as a competitive framework that can learn well-performing policies solely from pre-collected data with the help of learned dynamics models. To fully unleash the power of offline MBRL, model selection plays a pivotal role in determining the dynamics model utilized for downstream policy learning. However, offline MBRL conventionally relies on validation or off-policy evaluation, which are rather inaccurate due to the inherent distribution shift in offline RL. To tackle this, we propose BOMS, an active model selection framework that enhances model selection in offline MBRL with only a small online interaction budget, through the lens of Bayesian optimization (BO). Specifically, we recast model selection as BO and enable probabilistic inference in BOMS by proposing a novel model-induced kernel, which is theoretically grounded and computationally efficient. Through extensive experiments, we show that BOMS improves over the baseline methods with a small amount of online interaction comparable to only $1\%$-$2.5\%$ of offline training data on various RL tasks.
item.dc:creator: Yu-Wei Yang, Wei Hung, Yun-Ming Chan, Xi Liu, Ping-Chun Hsieh

item.title: A Bayesian Additive Regression Tree Model for Learning Conditional Average Treatment Effects in Regression Discontinuity Designs
item.description: arXiv:2503.00326v4 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: This paper develops an effective Bayesian approach to conditional average treatment effect (CATE) estimation in regression discontinuity designs (RDD), an increasingly prevalent form of quasi-experiment that facilitates causal inference. Earlier Bayesian approaches do not easily accommodate CATE estimation while recent frequentist approaches to this problem assume a known basis expansion, a steep model specification requirement that our approach avoids. The new model is a variant of a Bayesian additive regression tree (BART) model with linear leaf-level regressions on the running variable and a treatment dummy (and their interaction). The model adaptively partitions covariate space into regions where the slope on the running variable appreciably differs, providing interpretable Bayesian inference on conditional average treatment effects near the cutoff.
item.dc:creator: Rafael Alcantara, P. Richard Hahn, Hedibert F. Lopes

item.title: Federated Learning: From Theory to Practice
item.description: arXiv:2505.19183v3 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: This book offers a hands-on introduction to building and understanding federated learning (FL) systems. FL enables multiple devices -- such as smartphones, sensors, or local computers -- to collaboratively train machine learning (ML) models, while keeping their data private and local. It is a powerful solution when data cannot or should not be centralized due to privacy, regulatory, or technical reasons. The book is designed for students, engineers, and researchers who want to learn how to design scalable, privacy preserving FL systems. Our main focus is on personalization: enabling each device to train its own model while still benefiting from collaboration with relevant devices. This is achieved by leveraging similarities between (the learning tasks associated with) devices that are encoded by the weighted edges (or links) of a federated learning network (FL network). The key idea is to represent real-world FL systems as networks of devices, where nodes correspond to device and edges represent communication links and data similarities between them. The training of personalized models for these devices can be naturally framed as a distributed optimization problem. This optimization problem is referred to as generalized total variation minimization (GTVMin) and ensures that devices with similar learning tasks learn similar model parameters. Our approach is both mathematically principled and practically motivated. While we introduce some advanced ideas from optimization theory and graph-based learning, we aim to keep the book accessible. Readers are guided through the core ideas step by step, with intuitive explanations.
item.dc:creator: A. Jung

item.title: Recurrent Self-Attention Dynamics: An Energy-Agnostic Perspective from Jacobians
item.description: arXiv:2505.19458v5 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: The theoretical understanding of self-attention (SA) has been steadily progressing. A prominent line of work studies a class of SA layers that admit an energy function decreased by state updates. While it provides valuable insights into inherent biases in signal propagation, it often relies on idealized assumptions or additional constraints not necessarily present in standard SA. Thus, to broaden our understanding, this work aims to relax these energy constraints and provide an energy-agnostic characterization of inference dynamics by dynamical systems analysis. In more detail, we first consider relaxing the symmetry and single-head constraints traditionally required in energy-based formulations. Next, we show that analyzing the Jacobian matrix of the state is highly valuable when investigating more general SA architectures without necessarily admitting an energy function. It reveals that the normalization layer plays an essential role in suppressing the Lipschitzness of SA and the Jacobian's complex eigenvalues, which correspond to the oscillatory components of the dynamics. In addition, the Lyapunov exponents computed from the Jacobians demonstrate that the normalized dynamics lie close to a critical state, and this criticality serves as a strong indicator of high inference performance. Furthermore, the Jacobian perspective also enables us to develop regularization methods for training and a pseudo-energy for monitoring inference dynamics.
item.dc:creator: Akiyoshi Tomihari, Ryo Karakida

item.title: Solving Inverse Problems via Diffusion-Based Priors: An Approximation-Free Ensemble Sampling Approach
item.description: arXiv:2506.03979v3 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Diffusion models (DMs) have proven to be effective in modeling high-dimensional distributions, leading to their widespread adoption for representing complex priors in Bayesian inverse problems (BIPs). However, current DM-based posterior sampling methods proposed for solving common BIPs rely on heuristic approximations to the generative process. To exploit the generative capability of DMs and avoid the usage of such approximations, we propose an ensemble-based algorithm that performs posterior sampling without the use of heuristic approximations. Our algorithm is motivated by existing work that combines DM-based methods with the sequential Monte Carlo (SMC) method. By examining how the prior evolves through the diffusion process encoded by the pre-trained score function, we derive a modified partial differential equation (PDE) governing the evolution of the corresponding posterior distribution. This PDE includes a modified diffusion term and a reweighting term, which can be simulated via stochastic weighted particle methods. Theoretically, we prove that the error between the true posterior and the empirical distribution of the generated samples can be bounded in terms of the training error of the pre-trained score function and the number of particles in the ensemble. Empirically, we validate our algorithm on several inverse problems in imaging to show that our method gives more accurate reconstructions compared to existing DM-based methods. Our code is available at the following Github repository~\url{https://github.com/HaoxuanSteveC00/AFDPS-TMLR}.
item.dc:creator: Haoxuan Chen, Yinuo Ren, Martin Renqiang Min, Lexing Ying, Zachary Izzo

item.title: Universal Learning of Nonlinear Dynamics
item.description: arXiv:2508.11990v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: We study the fundamental problem of one-step prediction of a marginally stable unknown nonlinear dynamical system. We describe an algorithm for this problem, based on the technique of spectral filtering, which learns a mapping from past observations to the next based on a spectral representation of the system. Using techniques from online convex optimization, we prove vanishing prediction error for any nonexpansive nonlinear dynamical system with finitely many marginally stable modes, with rates governed by a novel quantitative control-theoretic notion of learnability. The main technical component of our method is a new spectral filtering algorithm for linear dynamical systems, which incorporates past observations and applies to general noisy and marginally stable systems. This generalizes the original spectral filtering algorithm to both asymmetric dynamics as well as incorporating noise correction, and is of independent interest.
item.dc:creator: Evan Dogariu, Anand Brahmbhatt, Elad Hazan

item.title: Distinguishability of causal structures under latent confounding and selection
item.description: arXiv:2509.20433v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Statistical relationships in observed data can arise for several different reasons: the observed variables may be causally related, they may share a latent common cause, or there may be selection bias. Each of these scenarios can be modelled using different causal graphs. Not all such causal graphs, however, can be distinguished by experimental data. In this paper, we formulate the equivalence class of causal graphs as a novel graphical structure, the selected-marginalized directed graph (smDG). That is, we show that two directed acyclic graphs with latent and selected vertices have the same smDG if and only if they are indistinguishable, even when allowing for arbitrary interventions on the observed variables. As a substitute for the more familiar d-separation criterion for DAGs, we provide an analogous sound and complete separation criterion in smDGs for conditional independence relative to passive observations. Finally, we provide a series of sufficient conditions under which two causal structures are indistinguishable when there is only access to passive observations.
item.dc:creator: Ryan Carey, Marina Maciel Ansanelli, Elie Wolfe, Robin J. Evans

item.title: Interpretable time series analysis with Gumbel dynamics
item.description: arXiv:2509.21578v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Switching dynamical systems can model complicated time series data while maintaining interpretability by inferring a finite set of dynamics primitives and explaining different portions of the observed time series with one of these primitives. However, due to the discrete nature of this set, such models struggle to capture smooth, variable-speed transitions, as well as stochastic mixtures of overlapping states (e.g., non-instantaneous state transitions), and the inferred dynamics often display spurious rapid switching on real-world datasets. Here, we propose the Gumbel Dynamical Model (GDM). First, by introducing a continuous relaxation of discrete states and a different noise model defined on the relaxed-discrete state space via the Gumbel distribution, GDM expands the set of available state dynamics, allowing the model to approximate smoother and non-stationary ground-truth dynamics more faithfully. Breaking from established literature, this new class uses a stochastic relaxed state to directly combine reusable dynamical primitives and govern observations, without a separate stochastic continuous trajectory. Second, the relaxation makes the model fully differentiable, enabling fast and scalable training with standard gradient descent methods. We validate our approach on standard simulation datasets and highlight its ability to model soft, sticky states and transitions in a stochastic setting. Furthermore, we apply our model to two real-world datasets, demonstrating its ability to infer interpretable states in stochastic time series with multiple dynamics, a setting where traditional methods often fail.
item.dc:creator: Yiliu Wang, Timothy Doyeon Kim, Eric Shea-Brown, Uygar S\"umb\"ul

item.title: Manifold Approximation leads to Robust Kernel Alignment
item.description: arXiv:2510.22953v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Centered kernel alignment (CKA) is a popular metric for comparing representations, determining equivalence of networks, and conducting neuroscience research. However, CKA does not account for the underlying manifold and relies on numerous heuristics that cause it to behave differently at different scales of data. In this work, we propose Manifold-approximated Kernel Alignment (MKA), which incorporates manifold geometry (i.e., local neighborhood) into the alignment task. We derive a theoretical framework for MKA. Our construction removes representation-dependent degree weighting, yields a closed-form alignment score, and gives each row a probabilistic interpretation as a local Markov transition distribution. We further establish kernel- and score-level stability with respect to the neighborhood size. We perform empirical evaluations on synthetic datasets and real-world examples to characterize and compare MKA to its contemporaries. In controlled synthetic experiments, MKA is consistently less sensitive to hyperparameters and captures the selected topology-preserving relationships. On the large-scale benchmark, MKA achieves its strongest aggregate performance in vision, is competitive on graphs, and is weaker than CKA in several NLP evaluations. Our findings suggest that manifold-aware kernel alignment provides a robust foundation for measuring representations and is potentially useful when local neighborhood geometry is important, with possible applications in representation learning.
item.dc:creator: Mohammad Tariqul Islam, Du Liu, Deblina Sarkar

item.title: A Stable Lasso
item.description: arXiv:2511.02306v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: The Lasso has been widely used as a method for variable selection, valued for its simplicity and empirical performance. However, Lasso's selection stability deteriorates in the presence of correlated predictors. Several approaches have been developed to mitigate this limitation. In this paper, we provide a brief review of existing approaches, highlighting their limitations. We then propose a technique to improve the selection stability of Lasso by integrating a weighting scheme into the Lasso penalty function, where the weights are defined as an increasing function of a correlation-adjusted ranking that reflects the predictive power of predictors. Empirical evaluations on both simulated and real-world datasets demonstrate the efficacy of the proposed method. Additional numerical results demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed approach in stabilizing other regularization-based selection methods, indicating its potential as a general-purpose solution.
item.dc:creator: Mahdi Nouraie, Houying Zhu, Samuel Muller

item.title: CLAPS: Aleatoric-Epistemic Scaling via Last-Layer Laplace for Conformal Regression
item.description: arXiv:2512.01384v5 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Conformal regression provides finite-sample marginal coverage, but interval efficiency depends on how uncertainty is allocated across inputs. We propose \emph{Conformal Laplace-Aware Predictive Scaling} (CLAPS), which combines a learned heteroscedastic scale with last-layer Laplace uncertainty. The learned variance also weights the training features used to construct the posterior, yielding a noise-weighted support correction in the learned representation. The correction contracts as weighted feature information increases and becomes most influential under localized support imbalance. Experiments show near-nominal marginal coverage and modest efficiency improvements over the matched aleatoric baseline on real regression benchmarks.
item.dc:creator: Dongseok Kim, Hyoungsun Choi, Mohamed Jismy Aashik Rasool, Gisung Oh

item.title: Ergodic Central limit theorem for subgeometric Markov chains
item.description: arXiv:2512.18255v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: We establish verifiable necessary conditions for central limit theorems (CLTs) of ergodic averages of Markov chains on general state spaces. Our criteria are based on discrete-time $\mathbf{L}$-drift conditions that can be verified through estimates for the one-step transition kernel of the original chain. They yield an integral criterion for failure of the CLT for a class of observables that includes unbounded functions and indicators of tail events. The main technical step transfers lower bounds for excursions of the original chain to regenerative excursions of its Nummelin split chain. The same drift conditions yield lower bounds on the tails of return times and modulated excursion functionals, on invariant tails, and on rates of convergence in $f$-variation and $L^p$-Wasserstein distance. These estimates apply without an explicit formula for the invariant distribution. Applications to unadjusted Langevin algorithms show preservation of polynomial target tail indices at every fixed step size. For Euler schemes with additive infinite-variance noise, we establish restrictions on invariant tails and transience under superlinear drifts. Schemes with linear drift, multiplicative noise and logarithmic innovation tails exhibit sharp polynomial convergence exponents and exact CLT thresholds, despite the absence of positive Euclidean moments.
item.dc:creator: Miha Bre\v{s}ar, Aleksandar Mijatovi\'c, Gareth Roberts

item.title: A probabilistic framework for irreversible kinetics
item.description: arXiv:2601.10763v3 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: A probabilistic framework for irreversible kinetics that unifies forward-in-time evolution and inverse inference, while quantifying epistemic uncertainty over admissible histories, is proposed. The forward-in-time evolution and inverse inference formulations differ only through observations and how they constrain admissible histories. All histories are ranked using a Gibbs-type probability measure $\exp(-\mathcal{J}/\Theta)$, where $\mathcal{J}$ encodes constitutive physics and observations. $\Theta$ controls epistemic uncertainty over the unknown histories, and the measure is interpreted as a Bayesian posterior over histories. Maximizing this posterior is equivalent to simultaneous minimization of $\mathcal{J}$ over the admissible history space. The framework is then specialized to generalized standard materials (GSM), for which $\mathcal{J}$ is constructed from incremental energy--dissipation functionals. This specialization reveals an important difference between the history resulting from simultaneous minimization over entire histories generally differs from the one generated by sequential GSM updates. Specifically, the causal GSM history incurs a higher history-level cost than the one obtained by simultaneous minimization, indicating that enforcing causality carries an additional cost at the history level. This difference is shown through seven representative examples: viscoelasticity, viscoplasticity, rate-independent plasticity, gradient damage, conserved and non-conserved phase transformations, and coupled thermoelectric evolution. Finally, the finite-$\Theta$ formulation is demonstrated on an inverse problem with a non-convex free energy, where incomplete initial-state information is used to infer unobserved intermediate states and quantify uncertainty over admissible histories. As $\Theta$ decreases, the posterior concentrates towards minimum-$\mathcal{J}$ histories.
item.arxiv:journal_reference: M. V. Upadhyay, Journal of the Mechanics and Physics of Solids (2026) 106875
item.dc:creator: Manas V. Upadhyay

item.title: Variance Reduction for Stochastic Switching in Functionally Constrained Federated Optimization
item.description: arXiv:2601.16897v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Federated learning (FL) is increasingly used in safety-critical and fairness-sensitive applications, where learning objectives must be optimized subject to functional constraints. This setting is challenging due to costly projection onto the resulting feasible set, stochastic constraint information, partial client participation, and limited communication at edge devices. We propose a federated stochastic switching framework based on primal-only updates, avoiding dual-variable tuning for functionally constrained federated optimization. For convex objectives, the framework further supports compression with error feedback to control compression-induced bias. We establish high-probability convergence and feasibility guarantees under stochastic gradients and partial client participation, and extend the analysis to weakly convex objectives through proximal-stationarity guarantees. Our bounds isolate the effects of stochastic gradients, constraint-evaluation noise, and partial participation, and show that direct switching can retain a nonvanishing constraint-estimation error even with exact local constraint evaluations. To overcome this limitation, we develop variance-reducing constraint estimators that yield vanishing feasibility and stationarity guarantees with fixed per-round client participation and constraint-evaluation batch sizes. Experiments on Neyman-Pearson classification, fairness-constrained learning on the ADULT dataset, and constrained deep reinforcement learning demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed framework.
item.dc:creator: Antesh Upadhyay, Sang Bin Moon, Zhankun Luo, Abolfazl Hashemi

item.title: Load Balancing with Evolving Workloads in Large-Scale Language Model Serving
item.description: arXiv:2601.17855v3 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Serving large language models requires assigning requests whose workloads grow during processing and whose completion times are unknown. With a synchronization barrier, lightly loaded workers wait for the slowest worker at every decode iteration. We model this loss through aggregate workload imbalance and formulate a joint admission and assignment problem with sticky requests and capacity limits. Short lookahead incorporates predicted completions of ongoing requests. For exact optimization without lookahead, we prove a comparison under independent geometric decode lengths, bounded independent nondegenerate prompt sizes, and batched releases satisfying a cumulative supply condition. The long-run expected imbalance improvement over first come, first served admission with request-count join-shortest-queue grows at least as the square root of the product of worker capacity and the logarithm of worker count, in the stated scaling regime. The comparison extends to capacity-aware round robin, random routing, and power of two choices. BalanceRoute approximations connect the formulation to practical routing. Experiments using up to 144 NPUs with proprietary and public traces show lower workload spread and higher throughput than the evaluated baselines. These empirical results complement the guarantee for exact optimization.
item.dc:creator: Zixi Chen, Tianci Bu, Chendong Song, Xin Lu, Yinyu Ye, Zijie Zhou

item.title: PTOPOFL: Topology-Guided Personalised Federated Learning with Persistent-Homology Client Descriptors
item.description: arXiv:2603.04323v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Clustered and personalised federated learning (FL) needs a signal telling the server which clients should share a model. Most methods derive it from losses or model updates that must be recomputed during training. We study pTopoFL, which derives it once, before training, from a compact persistent-homology (PH) descriptor of each client's feature distribution: the server clusters clients on these descriptors, weights them within clusters, and runs blended clustered local gradient descent, returning one personalised model per cluster. For strongly convex, smooth losses we analyse the complete procedure: for any partition, one round is a contraction with factor (1-eta*mu)^tau; the fixed point is characterised by a local-step drift bound, an exact formula for the effective strength of blending (which yields a calibration rule) and a stochastic floor exposing a bias-variance trade-off of clustering; and personalisation lowers the heterogeneity floor in proportion to a measurable share of the dispersion of client optima. Experiments on synthetic federations, a label-skew benchmark and a real four-hospital dataset confirm the theory and delimit the method. When feature geometry and decision rules co-vary, the PH partition recovers the latent client groups, including differences a linear-subspace descriptor misses, and pTopoFL is competitive with the strongest clustered baselines; on the real federation it lowers the test log-loss of FedAvg from 0.463 to 0.438, on par with the best personalised methods. When heterogeneity is invisible in feature geometry, it offers no advantage over FedAvg. pTopoFL transmits model parameters and is no more private than FedAvg; we give a record-level differential-privacy accounting and show that privatising the descriptor destroys the partition. Code reproduces every number.
item.dc:creator: Kelly L Vomo-Donfack, Adryel Hoszu, Gr\'egory Ginot, Ian Morilla

item.title: On the Role of Batch Size in Stochastic Conditional Gradient Methods
item.description: arXiv:2603.21191v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: We study the role of batch size in stochastic conditional gradient methods under a $\mu$-Kurdyka-{\L}ojasiewicz ($\mu$-KL) condition. Focusing on momentum-based stochastic conditional gradient algorithms (e.g., Scion), we derive a new analysis that explicitly captures the interaction between stepsize, batch size, and stochastic noise. Our study reveals a regime-dependent behavior: increasing the batch size initially improves optimization accuracy but, beyond a critical threshold, the benefits saturate and can eventually degrade performance under a fixed token budget. Notably, the theory predicts the magnitude of the optimal stepsize and aligns well with empirical practices observed in large-scale training. Leveraging these insights, we derive principled guidelines for selecting the batch size and stepsize, and propose an adaptive strategy that increases batch size and sequence length during training while preserving convergence guarantees. Experiments on NanoGPT are consistent with the theoretical predictions and illustrate the emergence of the predicted scaling regimes. Overall, our results provide a theoretical framework for understanding batch size scaling in stochastic conditional gradient methods and offer guidance for designing efficient training schedules in large-scale optimization.
item.arxiv:journal_reference: Proceedings of the 43rd International Conference on Machine Learning, Seoul, South Korea. PMLR 306, 2026
item.dc:creator: Rustem Islamov, Roman Machacek, Aurelien Lucchi, Antonio Silveti-Falls, Eduard Gorbunov, Volkan Cevher

item.title: Muon Dynamics as a Spectral Wasserstein Flow
item.description: arXiv:2604.04891v3 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Gradient normalization can stabilize deep-learning optimization, and spectral normalizations are especially natural for matrix-shaped parameter blocks; Muon is the motivating example. We study an idealized deterministic, continuous-time, vanishing-momentum version of this idea in the mean-field regime, where wide models are represented by probability measures on parameter space. Starting from normalized matrix flows, we introduce Spectral Wasserstein distances indexed by norms $\gamma$ on positive semidefinite matrices: the trace norm recovers the classical $W_2$ distance, the operator norm gives the Muon geometry, and Schatten norms interpolate between them. We develop a static Kantorovich formulation, a max--min robust-cost representation, and Gaussian reductions extending the Bures formula. For monotone norms, we prove equivalence with a Benamou--Brenier formulation and obtain a gradient-flow interpretation of normalized mean-field training dynamics. Numerical experiments illustrate the resulting flows for MMD objectives, Gaussian reductions, two-layer ReLU models, and shallow attention.
item.dc:creator: Gabriel Peyr\'e

item.title: Bandit Learning in General Open Multi-agent Systems
item.description: arXiv:2605.06202v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Open systems, where agents arrive and depart over time, are growing in digital platforms. Existing work on online learning in such systems, however, often relies on structural assumptions that may be restrictive in practice. In particular, heterogeneous rewards and general agent patterns create three new challenges: arrivals induce endogenous non-stationarity, agent patterns govern the rate of information accumulation, and uncertainty brought by new agents accumulates over time and scales regret. To this end, we formulate a learning problem for open systems that accommodates both forms of generality. We introduce new concepts to capture the inherent complexities: the \emph{pre-training degree} of new agents quantifies how much information an agent carries upon entry, \emph{stability} measures the impact of population changes on the global optimum, and \emph{global dynamic regret} compares the cumulative expected reward with that of the varying optimal arms. We also study a manifold representation of agents and introduce a \emph{dynamic population embedding} that directly encodes the population functional for each arm. We develop two UCB-based methods. The first combines entry information with online observations through agent-wise confidence bounds and aggregates the estimates and uncertainties for arm selection. The second pools agent-level observations through kernel regression on the manifold and constructs UCBs by projecting the confidence sets onto the current population embedding. Entry uncertainty enters the regret linearly through the pre-training error, while in stable regimes, regret is governed by the time needed to identify the stable optimal arm. With the manifold as a handle, regret is governed by the information gained from agent representations. These bounds all depend on population dynamics, but in different ways.
item.dc:creator: Mengfan Xu

item.title: Approximation Theory of Laplacian-Based Neural Operators for Reaction-Diffusion System
item.description: arXiv:2605.12025v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Neural operators provide a framework for learning solution operators of partial differential equations (PDEs), enabling efficient surrogate modeling for complex systems. While universal approximation results are now well understood, quantitative approximation analysis specific to nonlinear reaction-diffusion systems remains limited. In this paper, we study Laplacian-based neural operators applied to the solution mapping from initial conditions to time-dependent solutions of nonlinear reaction-diffusion systems. By exploiting the Laplacian spectral representation of the diffusion semigroup, we obtain polynomial complexity bounds on the network depth, width, and spectral rank, demonstrating that Laplacian eigenfunction-based neural operators can exploit the structure of the underlying PDE while avoiding the curse of parametric complexity encountered in generic operator learning. Numerical experiments support the theoretical findings and illustrate the benefit of Laplacian eigenfunction representations compared with Fourier-based spectral representations.
item.dc:creator: Takashi Furuya, Ryo Ozawa, Jenn-Nan Wang

item.title: Certifying Whether to Adapt: Baseline-Relative PAC-Bayes-MMD Guarantees for Test-Time Adaptation
item.description: arXiv:2605.21783v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Test-time adaptation (TTA) needs a decision about an update, not only an absolute-risk estimate. We give PAC-Bayesian certificates for the target excess risk of a candidate relative to a pilot-fixed baseline. A radial certificate uses an MMD ambiguity radius; a direction-sensitive certificate retains the sign of the empirical RKHS shift and can therefore certify target improvement even when source risk increases. For finite binary state spaces we derive statewise marginal and signed conditional-shift refinements, with penalties localized to candidate--baseline disagreements. A source-worsening update with target excess risk $-0.576$ is accepted in all 1,000 repetitions by the directional certificate and never by the radial certificate; learned finite-state updates with excess risks $-0.800$ and $-0.401$ are likewise accepted in every repetition. On Covertype, the certificate safely rejects all updates and blocks geographic-shift adaptations whose unconditional deployment increases risk by up to $2.75$ percentage points in prespecified base libraries; an exploratory stress test reaches $5.66$ points. A feature-quantized CIFAR-10-C and ImageNet-C study is structurally vacuous and is reported only as a diagnostic limitation, not as a practical neural certificate.
item.dc:creator: Ahanaf Hasan Ariq, Hasaan Ahmad, Aayush Parekh, Abdul Monaf Chowdhury

item.title: Service-Induced Congestion in Memory-Constrained LLM Serving
item.description: arXiv:2606.15555v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: In large language model (LLM) serving, each request accumulates persistent graphics processing unit (GPU) memory during service as its key-value cache grows with every generated token. Under high concurrency, aggregate memory usage therefore increases endogenously over time: the service process itself creates future capacity pressure. When memory capacity is exceeded, systems evict active requests, discarding cached state and restarting them later, which wastes computation and reduces throughput. We develop a discrete-time dynamical model of memory-constrained LLM inference that captures admission, memory growth, and eviction under continuous batching. In the saturated-input regime, the system admits both eviction-free fixed points and limit cycles with evictions. For homogeneous workloads, we show that the eviction-free equilibrium is unstable and that, except for a Lebesgue-measure-zero exact-capture set, the system converges to a unique worst-case limit cycle that is asymptotically stable outside this exceptional set, with throughput losses as large as 50%. For heterogeneous workloads, we prove a stability criterion in the two-class common-input setting and explain how the survival-polynomial mechanism generalizes to multiple classes and heterogeneous-input lengths. Under an input-dominated scaling regime, coprime decoding lengths stabilize the eviction-free equilibrium, while non-coprime lengths create synchronized modes that drive instability. These results characterize when workload heterogeneity desynchronizes completions and helps stabilize memory-constrained serving. More broadly, we identify service-induced congestion as a structural instability mechanism and derive scheduling design principles for sustaining high throughput.
item.dc:creator: Ruicheng Ao, Jing Dong, Gan Luo, David Simchi-Levi

item.title: A Decision-Theoretic View of Test-Time Training: When, How Far, and Which Directions to Adapt
item.description: arXiv:2606.15569v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Test-time training (TTT) adapts a pretrained model to each prompt via parameter updates, improving accuracy under pretraining-to-test distribution shifts. Yet, its performance often suffers from instability and sensitivity to hyperparameters such as update steps and subspace. We explain this behavior through a decision-theoretic lens, treating TTT as implicit Bayesian inference in the kernel regime. Under a Gaussian process benchmark, we show that TTT reduces prediction error when updates are spectrally matched to the prompt's signal-to-noise ratio and aligned with query-relevant eigen-directions. This perspective underpins the following results: (1) we show when fixed update steps and subspaces fail under distribution shifts, motivating adaptive strategies; (2) we prove that selecting update steps via prompt evidence admits a PAC-Bayes guarantee against overfitting; and (3) we characterize the Bayes-optimal update subspace under a linear-Gaussian correction model, yielding a scoring rule for selecting Transformer blocks and heads. Our theory helps explain the empirical instability of TTT, taking a step toward principled guidance for when, how far, and which directions to adapt.
item.dc:creator: Tomoya Wakayama

item.title: On the Role of Normalization in Binary Iterative Hard Thresholding for 1-bit Compressed Sensing
item.description: arXiv:2607.15530v3 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Binary Iterative Hard Thresholding (BIHT) is a simple, yet effective, greedy method for recovering a sparse vector from one-bit sign measurements. In its original form, BIHT performs a ``gradient-descent'' step, followed by hard thresholding. A convergence analysis of this algorithm was left open in the introductory work of Jacques, Laska, Boufounos, and Baraniuk [IEEE Trans. Inform. Theory (2013)] and has remained unresolved for over a decade, with subsequent sharp analyses studying a {\em normalized variant} instead, that additionally projects every iterate onto the unit sphere. This paper resolves that gap and characterizes when per-iteration normalization is algorithmically necessary. In the noiseless setting, we prove a universal, sample-optimal convergence theorem for the original BIHT algorithm. Specifically, with $\widetilde O(s/\epsilon)$ measurements, a deterministic, computable finite-time iterate has directional error at most $\epsilon$, simultaneously for every $s$-sparse unit vector. This matches the optimal sample dependence achieved by normalized BIHT in prior work. Under sign corruptions, we prove a sharp separation. If at most a $\tau$ fraction of signs are flipped adversarially, then BIHT, without per-iterate normalization, still reaches the robust error floor at an early iterate with a matching $\widetilde O(s/\epsilon)$ sample complexity rate as its normalized variant. This recovery, however, is not stable. We prove a scalar lower bound showing that any nontrivial corruption pattern, even one that involves only one flipped sign together with one clean sign, forces the iterates to oscillate indefinitely. Consequently, no general last-iterate convergence theorem can hold for BIHT under sign corruptions, while its normalized surrogate provably escapes this instance.
item.dc:creator: Arya Mazumdar, Prateeti Mukherjee

item.title: Deep Stochastic Residual Methods for Fully Nonlinear Parabolic Equations
item.description: arXiv:2607.16730v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: We develop and analyze neural stochastic residual methods for fully nonlinear parabolic terminal problems under exact diffusion sampling. A quadratic stochastic residual supports global training and backward regression with scalar networks and losses involving only spatial derivatives. For global training, the correction removes a Hessian penalty from the limiting first-order loss. Under a uniform output regularity budget, we bound the continuous residual norm by the square roots of the global loss or normalized backward-regression excess loss, an $O(h^{1/2})$ discretization term for time step $h$, and terminal error. Residual stability then gives value, gradient and Hessian error bounds. Under suitable solution and terminal assumptions, we construct admissible networks with $O(h^{1/2})$ bounds on these approximation errors and the square roots of both loss criteria. In ten-dimensional backward-regression tests using a shared schedule tuned for the quadratic residual, mean relative Hessian errors are $5$--$6\%$ with the quadratic residual and about $15\%$ with the first-order residual. Tuned backward regression achieves Hessian accuracy comparable to physics-informed neural networks across the tested nonlinear coefficients. Translation tests show that the ratio of Hessian error to residual can grow sharply under a fixed sampling law.
item.dc:creator: Zhenhua Zhao, Jihao Long

item.title: Test-Time Augmentation for LLMs: Where to Inject Diversity at Inference Time
item.description: arXiv:2608.09351v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Aggregating several LLM responses to the same question can improve accuracy, but every method that does so must decide where the responses should differ. Established test-time scaling methods such as self-consistency vary only the reasoning path, resampling from a fixed input. The input modification offers several further options: the wording of the question can be rephrased, the spelling can be perturbed, and the accompanying images can be transformed. We study Test-Time Augmentation (TTA), which aggregates predictions across transformed versions of the input, and use it to ask where diversity is best injected. Comparing these options across six benchmarks at a matched number of inference calls, we find that where the diversity comes from matters more than how much of it there is. Meaning-preserving paraphrases of the input yield the largest accuracy gains (+1.80 pp over a single call) and reach peak accuracy with the fewest samples. Yet, they are not the most diverse: character-level noise makes the responses disagree far more often (37.8% versus 27.4%) while gaining less accuracy, and perturbing two modalities at once falls below the single-call baseline. Not all diversity is equally useful: perturbations that keep the meaning intact produce disagreement that aggregation can use, while those that corrupt it produce disagreement that is wrong. Overall, our results suggest that for mid-tier LLMs such as Claude Haiku, varying how a question is phrased is a better use of an inference call than varying the reasoning path. Our TTA implementation is available at github.com/aws-samples/sample-genai-reflection-for-bedrock.
item.dc:creator: Nikita Kozodoi, Zainab Afolabi, Jack Butler

item.title: An RKHS Framework for Fixed Effects in Permanental Process Models
item.description: arXiv:2608.17908v3 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: This short work describes an extension of the permanental process model which includes fixed effects. By starting with a prior on the fixed effects coefficients we show that, in the diffuse prior limit, the intensity function of the permanental process can be found using the representer theorem and naturally decomposed into a fixed effects term and a function which is an element of a Reproducing Kernel Hilbert Space (RKHS). We show that the limiting equivalent kernel defines an RKHS whose squared norm is exactly the limiting penalty. This allows for straightforward scientific interpretation of permanental process models and the easy incorporation of domain knowledge into the estimation process.
item.dc:creator: Matthew LeDuc

item.title: When Clean Data Hurts: Learning with Monotone Corruptions Beyond Binary Classification
item.description: arXiv:2608.20480v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Optimal learners are tailored to exploit the i.i.d.\ data assumption underlying the classic PAC model. What if an i.i.d.\ training sample were corrupted with correctly labeled examples drawn from an otherwise unrelated, even adversarial source? This model of learning with monotone adversarial corruptions was recently introduced by Larsen et al. (2026), who demonstrated that all known optimal binary learners suffer increased error rates in this setting, from $O(d / n)$ in the PAC model to $\Omega (d \log(n / d) / n)$ under monotone corruption. Mehrotra (2026) proved this logarithmic factor to be necessary for binary classification, but left open the consequences of corruption for more general learning settings, such as multiclass classification and partial binary concept classes. As our primary result, we demonstrate that monotone adversaries are frighteningly more powerful in each of these settings. We exhibit a learnable multiclass problem, of DS dimension only 2, that becomes altogether unlearnable under a monotone adversary, and show an analogous result for partial binary concept classes. These results are achieved by an adaptive adversary permitted to view the original i.i.d.\ training set $S$ and to insert $b < \infty$ corrupted datapoints into $S$. In the multiclass example, the adversary need only insert a linear number $b = |S| = n$ of datapoints. We complement these impossibility results by proving that every class remains learnable when the number of adaptive additions is $o(n)$, which our previous multiclass lower bound proves to be tight. We further observe that the classic multiclass error rate of $O(d_{\mathrm{DS}} / n)$ remains achievable against adaptive adversaries restricted to a known constant budget $b = O(1)$, against semi-adaptive adversaries viewing only a $p$-fraction of $S$ for $p \in (0, 1)$, and against oblivious adversaries that cannot view $S$.
item.dc:creator: Julian Asilis, Shaddin Dughmi, Chirag Pabbaraju

item.title: ICON decomposition: Multivariate concept auditing reveals shortcuts that neural networks rely on
item.description: arXiv:2608.26083v5 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Deep neural networks often exploit spurious associations, a failure known as shortcut learning. Before deployment, models should therefore be audited for reliance on concepts such as acquisition artifacts and patient demographics. Current methods, including linear probes and concept activation vectors, measure concept reliance by asking whether each concept is decodable from a layer. We show that this framing is misleading: decodability reflects not only concept reliance but also correlations among concepts and the outcome in the auditing dataset. We reframe shortcut auditing as a decomposition of the variance of intermediary representations with Independent Canonical cONcepts (ICON).
